title: Support passing existing functions to `crate()`
description:
## Background: the "fresh function" requirement

Since the original implementation in 2018, `crate()` has required `.fn` to be "fresh", i.e. defined lexically inside the `crate()` call:

```r
fn <- function(x) toupper(x)
crate(fn)
#> Error: The function must be defined inside this call
```

Mechanically, `.fn` is captured unevaluated and evaluated inside the crate's new evaluation environment. A function literal written in the call therefore has that environment as its enclosure by construction, and `crate()` enforces freshness with an identity check:

```r
if (!is_reference(get_env(fn), env)) {
  abort("The function must be defined inside this call")
}
```

The error message in the first draft of this check was "Can't supply an evaluated function" (reworded in ad1919e), which makes the original design intent clear: `.fn` was conceived as an unevaluated argument, so that the function is *born* self-contained in a controlled environment rather than retrofitted after the fact.

The restriction was a deliberate fail-loud design with three motivations:

1. **A closure's environment is part of its semantics.** Silently reparenting an existing closure breaks any function that legitimately depends on its lexical scope — closures produced by function factories or `local()` lose their captured state, and functions relying on attached packages lose search-path access. The failure would surface only at call time, typically on a remote worker where an "object not found" error is hardest to diagnose.

2. **Blanket reparenting is flatly wrong for some functions.** Setting the environment of a namespaced function strips its namespace, breaking every internal lookup of unexported helpers. Primitives have no environment to set at all, and attaching attributes to them is deprecated.

3. **The workaround is informed consent.** The docs have always suggested `crate(rlang::set_env(fn))` as the escape hatch. Writing it yourself is an assertion that `fn` does not depend on its enclosure and takes all of its data from `...`. (It only works through a subtlety: the expression is evaluated inside the crate environment, so `set_env()`'s default `new_env = caller_env()` resolves to the crate environment, which then passes the identity check.)

## What changed since: functions passed via `...` are auto-crated

carrier 0.3.0 crossed this line for helper functions. Since #28, closures passed via `...` have their enclosing environment silently replaced with the crate's evaluation environment — exactly the automatic `set_env()` treatment that the freshness check was designed to prevent for `.fn`. #13 / #33 refined this so that existing crates passed via `...` are left untouched.

That leaves the API in an inconsistent position: a helper passed *alongside* the main function is reparented automatically, while the main function itself requires explicit ceremony to opt in to the same behaviour. The safety argument for the ceremony is hard to sustain when the package already applies the transformation silently one argument over.

Two further points in favour of relaxing the requirement:

* **The residual hazard is deterministic and locally testable.** Because the crate environment's parent is `baseenv()` either way, a reparented closure that is missing data fails identically in a local test call and on a remote worker. It is not a "works here, breaks there" trap, and the docs already recommend smoke-testing crates by calling them.

* **Ergonomics.** Users coming from `purrr`, `parallel`, `future`, or `mirai` expect to pass existing functions directly. Requiring `crate(function(x) fn(x), fn = fn)` or knowledge of the `set_env()` trick is a recurring paper cut.

## Proposal

Accept existing functions in `.fn`, with type-appropriate handling rather than a blanket `set_env()`:

* **Plain closures** have their enclosing environment replaced with the crate's evaluation environment — equivalent to the long-documented `crate(rlang::set_env(fn))` workaround, and consistent with how `...` closures are treated since 0.3.0.

* **Namespace functions and primitives** are wrapped in a thin closure that delegates to them, leaving their original environment untouched. This preserves internal namespace lookups and avoids the deprecation warning when setting attributes on primitives.

* **Existing crates** are passed through unchanged, consistent with #33.

* **Unreachable data is an error.** Data declared via `...` is only reachable from plain closures, so supplying `...` together with an existing crate, a namespace function, or a primitive errors at crate time rather than silently producing dead bindings.

## Trade-off

The one case where the new behaviour is strictly worse than the old error is closures that depend on captured state, e.g. function-factory results:

```r
fn <- stats::ecdf(1:10)
crated <- crate(fn)
crated(5)
#> Error in .approxfun(...): could not find function ".approxfun"
```

Previously this failed loudly at crate time; now it fails at call time. carrier cannot reliably distinguish a factory closure from a user closure (any heuristic based on the environment chain misclassifies closures defined in testthat or knitr contexts, which inherit from a namespace). Since the failure is deterministic and reproduces locally, the proposal is to document this pitfall prominently with an example rather than guess.

title: Recomended pattern for functions that need an `init` hook?
description:
In ragnar we accept an `embed` function. We serialize this function and store it in a DuckDB database. The `embed` function’s job is to take a character vector and return a matrix.

Most `embed` functions currently call an HTTP API where an embedding model is hosted, so no complex setup is needed, and simple usage of `crate()` works well.

It would be useful to support `embed` functions that use a local, in-process embedding model. For this pattern, it would be ideal to have a first-run init hook after restoring the function. For example:

```r
reticulate::py_require("sentence-transformers")
model <- reticulate::import("sentence_transformers")$SentenceTransformer(
  "google/embeddinggemma-300m"
)
embed <- function(x) {
  model$encode_query(x)
}
```

Or more simply:

```r
embed <- model$encode_query
```

Note that serializing `model` is not an option, as it's just an external pointer.

I’m wondering if you've encountered a similar need before, and whether carrier can help.

title: Returning a multi row data frame?
description:
Hi, 

I would like my function to return a data frame, but I can't seem to figure out how to do this either via `in_parallel` or via `crate`. Here's a reprex. Some setup code:

``` r
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
library(purrr)
library(carrier)
library(mirai)
library(rlang)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'rlang'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:purrr':
#> 
#>     %@%, flatten, flatten_chr, flatten_dbl, flatten_int, flatten_lgl,
#>     flatten_raw, invoke, splice

c("dplyr", "purrr", "carrier", "mirai", "rlang") %>%
  set_names(nm = ~ .x) %>%
  map(.f = ~ packageVersion(.x))
#> $dplyr
#> [1] '1.1.4'
#> 
#> $purrr
#> [1] '1.1.0'
#> 
#> $carrier
#> [1] '0.2.0'
#> 
#> $mirai
#> [1] '2.4.1'
#> 
#> $rlang
#> [1] '1.1.4'

iris_tbl <- iris %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  mutate(row_id = row_number())

helper_function <- function(x) {
 x %>% exp() %>% log()
}

slice_df_single_row <- function(z) {
  Sys.sleep(1)
  z <- helper_function(z)
  iris_tbl %>%
    dplyr::slice(z)
}

slice_df_multiple_rows <- function(z) {
  Sys.sleep(1)
  z <- helper_function(z)
  start <- z + 10
  end <- start + 3
  iris_tbl %>%
    dplyr::slice(start:end)
}

slice_df_single_row(5)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 6
#>   Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Petal.Length Petal.Width Species row_id
#>          <dbl>       <dbl>        <dbl>       <dbl> <fct>    <int>
#> 1            5         3.6          1.4         0.2 setosa       5
slice_df_multiple_rows(5)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 6
#>   Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Petal.Length Petal.Width Species row_id
#>          <dbl>       <dbl>        <dbl>       <dbl> <fct>    <int>
#> 1          5.8         4            1.2         0.2 setosa      15
#> 2          5.7         4.4          1.5         0.4 setosa      16
#> 3          5.4         3.9          1.3         0.4 setosa      17
#> 4          5.1         3.5          1.4         0.3 setosa      18

system.time({test_seq_single <- map_dfr(.x = 1:5, .f = ~ slice_df_single_row(.x))})
#>    user  system elapsed 
#>   0.020   0.001   5.024
test_seq_single
#> # A tibble: 5 × 6
#>   Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Petal.Length Petal.Width Species row_id
#>          <dbl>       <dbl>        <dbl>       <dbl> <fct>    <int>
#> 1          5.1         3.5          1.4         0.2 setosa       1
#> 2          4.9         3            1.4         0.2 setosa       2
#> 3          4.7         3.2          1.3         0.2 setosa       3
#> 4          4.6         3.1          1.5         0.2 setosa       4
#> 5          5           3.6          1.4         0.2 setosa       5

system.time({test_seq_multiple <- map_dfr(.x = 1:5, .f = ~ slice_df_multiple_rows(.x))})
#>    user  system elapsed 
#>   0.020   0.001   5.027
test_seq_multiple
#> # A tibble: 20 × 6
#>    Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Petal.Length Petal.Width Species row_id
#>           <dbl>       <dbl>        <dbl>       <dbl> <fct>    <int>
#>  1          5.4         3.7          1.5         0.2 setosa      11
#>  2          4.8         3.4          1.6         0.2 setosa      12
#>  3          4.8         3            1.4         0.1 setosa      13
#>  4          4.3         3            1.1         0.1 setosa      14
#>  5          4.8         3.4          1.6         0.2 setosa      12
#>  6          4.8         3            1.4         0.1 setosa      13
#>  7          4.3         3            1.1         0.1 setosa      14
#>  8          5.8         4            1.2         0.2 setosa      15
#>  9          4.8         3            1.4         0.1 setosa      13
#> 10          4.3         3            1.1         0.1 setosa      14
#> 11          5.8         4            1.2         0.2 setosa      15
#> 12          5.7         4.4          1.5         0.4 setosa      16
#> 13          4.3         3            1.1         0.1 setosa      14
#> 14          5.8         4            1.2         0.2 setosa      15
#> 15          5.7         4.4          1.5         0.4 setosa      16
#> 16          5.4         3.9          1.3         0.4 setosa      17
#> 17          5.8         4            1.2         0.2 setosa      15
#> 18          5.7         4.4          1.5         0.4 setosa      16
#> 19          5.4         3.9          1.3         0.4 setosa      17
#> 20          5.1         3.5          1.4         0.3 setosa      18
```

The code works fine in sequential, takes the expected amount of time to run (5 seconds), and returns the desired results in both cases.

Run single row function in parallel

``` r
daemons(5)
#> [1] 5

test_env <- env(
  `%>%` = magrittr::`%>%`,
  helper_function = helper_function,
  slice_df_single_row = slice_df_single_row,
  slice_df_multiple_rows = slice_df_multiple_rows
)

crate_obj_single <- crate(function(z) slice_df_single_row(z), .parent_env = test_env)
crate_obj_single
#> <crate> 13.98 kB
#> * function: 392 B
#> function (z) 
#> slice_df_single_row(z)

system.time({test_par_single <- crate_obj_single(1:5)})
#>    user  system elapsed 
#>   0.003   0.000   1.003
test_par_single
#> # A tibble: 5 × 6
#>   Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Petal.Length Petal.Width Species row_id
#>          <dbl>       <dbl>        <dbl>       <dbl> <fct>    <int>
#> 1          5.1         3.5          1.4         0.2 setosa       1
#> 2          4.9         3            1.4         0.2 setosa       2
#> 3          4.7         3.2          1.3         0.2 setosa       3
#> 4          4.6         3.1          1.5         0.2 setosa       4
#> 5          5           3.6          1.4         0.2 setosa       5
```

In the case where the function returns a single row, I'm assuming it works correctly - I get 5 rows but the execution time is 1 second instead of 5.

Is this approach using `rlang::env()` acceptable for specifying the subset of objects from the `globalenv` that we'd like to pass to the executors? I find this cleaner than the nested function approach (mentioned [here](https://github.com/tidyverse/purrr/issues/1200#issuecomment-3061893103)) of defining all my functions within my main function (called `run_pipeline()`) as that could get quite long since I have about 7 functions in total.

Now with multiple rows, we get a warrning that only the first element is used - and indeed only the result for `crate_obj_multiple(1)` is returned.

``` r
crate_obj_multiple <- crate(function(z) slice_df_multiple_rows(z), .parent_env = test_env)
crate_obj_multiple
#> <crate> 13.98 kB
#> * function: 392 B
#> function (z) 
#> slice_df_multiple_rows(z)

system.time({test_par_multiple <- crate_obj_multiple(1:5)})
#> Warning in start:end: numerical expression has 5 elements: only the first used
#>    user  system elapsed 
#>   0.003   0.000   1.004
test_par_multiple
#> # A tibble: 4 × 6
#>   Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Petal.Length Petal.Width Species row_id
#>          <dbl>       <dbl>        <dbl>       <dbl> <fct>    <int>
#> 1          5.4         3.7          1.5         0.2 setosa      11
#> 2          4.8         3.4          1.6         0.2 setosa      12
#> 3          4.8         3            1.4         0.1 setosa      13
#> 4          4.3         3            1.1         0.1 setosa      14

daemons(0)
#> [1] 0
```

<sup>Created on 2025-07-30 with [reprex v2.1.1](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

Is there a way that I can get the same result as `test_seq_multiple` above either using in_parallel + some map function or via crate, or is this currently not possible?

Thanks!

title: Switch function closures to the local environment
description:
When functions are supplied to the `...` of `crate()`:

This fixes the following problem, when functions defined in the global environment are passed:
- Function closure is the global environment, so it will only look  for non-local variables there
- This means anything else passed via `...` and defined in our local environment (e.g. helper functions) will not be found

This is what is happening at https://github.com/tidyverse/purrr/issues/1172 and https://github.com/tidyverse/purrr/issues/1200.

title: Crated functions do not find packages attached by `library()`
description:
In the context of `purrr::in_parallel()` which is a thin wrapper of `carrier::crate()`.

Raised by @DavisVaughan on Slack:

```r
library(purrr)
mirai::daemons(5)
walk(
  1:10,
  .progress = TRUE,
  in_parallel(\(x) {
    library(ggplot2)
    p <- penguins |>
      ggplot(aes(bill_len, bill_dep)) +
      geom_point()
    ggsave(paste0("x", x, ".png"))
    Sys.sleep(2) # To have time to interact
  })
)
```
Errors with:
```r
#> Error in `map()` at purrr/R/map.R:264:3:
#> ℹ In index: 1.
#> Caused by error in `ggplot()`:
#> ! could not find function "ggplot"
#> Run `rlang::last_trace()` to see where the error occurred.
```
Even though a `library()` call is made within the function, as the crate's environment is isolated from the search path, the package functions aren't found.

This is the case no matter if the crated function is run locally or in a parallel process. They currently require _all_ functions to be namespaced, which is not always convenient.

title: Problem crating a lightgbm model
description:
Hi,

First of all, thank you for your amazing work. I have been able to log a lightgbm model in mlflow using a "crated" function. Problem is, when I load the crated model in a new, clean, session, I have problems as some of the dependencies are not there.

I have started declaring each of the dependencies that were rising errors by hand, to see if I could arrive to a decent compromise, but I am encountering some problems once I arrive to some FFI code. 

Say I have a fitted workflow model...

```
> final_fit
══ Workflow [trained] ═══════════
Preprocessor: Recipe
Model: boost_tree()

── Preprocessor ──────────────────
0 Recipe Steps

── Model ────────────────
LightGBM Model (1174 trees)
Objective: binary
Fitted to dataset with 25 columns
> 
```

...and I try to crate a function for prediction in the following way:

```
c_model <- crate(
    function(new_obs) get_predictions(model, new_obs),
    model = final_fit,
    get_predictions = rlang::set_env(rchurn2:::get_predictions),
    predict = rlang::set_env(workflows:::predict.workflow),
    is_trained_workflow = rlang::set_env(workflows:::is_trained_workflow),
    validate_is_workflow = rlang::set_env(workflows:::validate_is_workflow),
    check_dots_empty = rlang::set_env(rlang::check_dots_empty),
    ellipsis_dots = rlang::set_env(rlang:::ellipsis_dots),
    ffi_ellipsis_dots = rlang:::ffi_ellipsis_dots,
    caller_env = rlang::set_env(rlang::caller_env)
)
```

Then, if I try to call it in a clean session, it is giving me some error I just cannot understand:

```
callr::r(
    function (d, cmod) {
        cmod(d)
    },
    args = list(
        d = splits[['tst']],
        cmod = c_model
    )
)

Error: 
! in callr subprocess.
Caused by error in `.Call(ffi_ellipsis_dots, env)`:
! NULL value passed as symbol address
Type .Last.error to see the more details.
> 
```

Just wanted to know if I am trying to do too much (if it is possible to crate functions depending on FFI code), or if it would be better just to ensure that all needed dependencies are available in the machine that is going to run the inference part. The latter would be the easy and comfortable path, but I just wanted to know, because I think crate is a great tool, and this is not such a corner case.

Thanks a lot in advance. 

Gus.

title: renv support for crated functions
description:
While carrier captures some dependencies, it's limited in the sense that it does not capture package and R versions. This might be a very crucial part in reproducibility as well as when using `crate` functions in a deployment context but also when sending these functions to a remote worker. A potential application is the deployment of `crate` functions in `mlflow`, as partly discussed in [these issues](https://github.com/mlflow/mlflow/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aopen+renv). At the moment, R deployment with AWS or Azure ML is not supported, the Python deployment method rely on `conda` for dependency management. I think it would be great if there was a way to create a `renv` environment from a crated function, bridging the gap between renv and carrier. E.g. like this
```r
fn <- carrier::crate(function(x) styler::style_text(x))
carrier::burry(fn, ...)
```
Where `burry()` would save a `renv.lock` (or set up all required files/directories to later use `renv::restore()`) derived from `fn` and the current library (potentially already managed by renv). I am not sure there are some internals from `renv` that had to be exported from the package to leverage `renv` to discover the dependencies in the crated functions and write the lockfile or if this issue should rather go to rstudio/renv.

cc: @mdneuzerling

title: Move `master` branch to `main`
description:
The `master` branch of this repository will soon be renamed to `main`, as part of a coordinated change across several GitHub organizations (including, but not limited to: [tidyverse](https://github.com/tidyverse), [r-lib](https://github.com/r-lib), [tidymodels](https://github.com/tidymodels), and [sol-eng](https://github.com/sol-eng)). We anticipate this will happen by the end of September 2021.

That will be preceded by a release of the [usethis package](https://usethis.r-lib.org), which will gain some functionality around detecting and adapting to a renamed default branch. There will also be a blog post at the time of this `master` --> `main` change.

The purpose of this issue is to:

* Help us firm up the list of targetted repositories
* Make sure all maintainers are aware of what's coming
* Give us an issue to close when the job is done
* Give us a place to put advice for collaborators re: how to adapt
